title: Closed-loop stability, gain and phase margins

sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
Feedback can make a stable plant unstable. A closed loop is stable when every pole of \(A = a/(1 + T)\), the roots of \(1 + T(s) = 0\), lies in the left half-plane. Finding those roots directly works for simple loops, but the frequency response of \(T\) gives a more useful view.

Trouble comes when the loop returns a signal inverted by an extra \(180^\circ\) with a gain of one or more: negative feedback has turned positive. Two **margins** measure how far a loop is from that point. The **phase margin** is \(180^\circ\) plus the phase of \(T\) at the gain crossover, where \(|T| = 1\). The **gain margin** is how much the gain could rise before \(|T| = 1\) at the frequency where the phase reaches \(-180^\circ\). The **Nyquist plot** of \(T(j\omega)\) shows both: the distance from the curve to the point \(-1\) is the robustness.

Small margins mean ringing and overshoot in the closed-loop step response. A phase margin of about \(45^\circ\) to \(60^\circ\) is a common target. A pure time delay adds phase lag that grows with frequency, so it eats phase margin.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: Take \(T(s) = 6/(s(s + 2))\). At crossover \(\omega_c\sqrt{\omega_c^2 + 4} = 6\) gives \(\omega_c \approx 2.08\ \mathrm{rad/s}\). The phase is \(-90^\circ - \arctan(1.04) = -136.1^\circ\), so the phase margin is about \(44^\circ\). The phase never reaches \(-180^\circ\), so the gain margin is infinite.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Measuring phase margin at the wrong frequency.
- Assuming a large gain margin implies a good phase margin.
- Ignoring delay when the loop crossover is fast.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Margins are the design targets for loop shaping and compensation, both in amplifiers and in control loops.
